dialogue.english: Because of working hard, he received a reward.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Nekuda [and / with kuda] • kwekushanda [kwekushanda] • nesimba [and / with simba] • akawana [he/she (past) wana] • mubayiro [in / singular bayiro]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akawana')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akawana' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'Nekuda'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'Nekuda'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'kuda' forms 'Nekuda'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Nekuda kwekushanda nesimba, akawana mubayiro.', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

cultural_notes.title: Honouring Hard Work ('Kushanda Nesimba') & Academic/Work Awards ('Mubayiro')
cultural_notes.content: Schools, churches, and workplaces in Zimbabwe hold annual prize-giving days to award prizes ('mubayiro') to students and workers who have distinguished themselves through diligence ('kushanda nesimba').

active_exercises.prompt: How would you say 'Open the door quickly!' in Shona using the vocabulary pattern from this unit?
Translate this new sentence into English: 'Tora mvura uinwe.'
options: Take the water and drink it.
Put the cup on the table before you leave.
Close the window because it is cold outside.
Come here and help me carry the books.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Take the water and drink it.

active_exercises.prompt: Why do we say 'Mbuya vari kurima' instead of 'Mbuya ari kurima' when talking about one grandmother?
options: Because 'mbuya' always refers to three or more people
Shona uses the plural prefix 'va-' ('vari') to show polite respect to elders and parents
Because 'vari' is only used for the future tense
Because 'ari' can only be used with inanimate objects
active_exercises.correct_answer: Shona uses the plural prefix 'va-' ('vari') to show polite respect to elders and parents
active_exercises.explanation: In Shona, respected family elders ('amai', 'baba', 'mbuya', 'sekuru') always take the polite plural 'va-' agreement.
